 Folk versus Frazier: The Hennepin County Attorney’s race could mean the difference between life and death
 As students contend with crime around the University of Minnesota’s surrounding neighborhoods, one unassuming election could decide the future of public safety within the region. 
 Categories: 
 Candidate Profiles 
 City 
 City Life 
 Marquee 
 Midterms 
 Top Story 
 by Jo Larson and Maddie Mullikin 
 Published November 2, 2026 
 She was dressed as Strawberry Shortcake when gunshots woke her up.  
 It was 2 a.m. on Nov. 1, 2025, overshadowing a night of Halloween celebrations.  
 A body was sprawled over the sidewalk on 13th Avenue Southeast where, just hours earlier, Ella Albrecht had walked home from Mesa Pizza. 
 She had fallen asleep after a late-night mac and cheese slice, but 20 automatic gunshots shattered the silence of her sixth-floor bedroom.  
 She ran out to her balcony, half awake, and watched as a man ran from the scene holding a gun. Five others ran toward the man’s body, ripping his shirt off to perform CPR. Later, after the man was declared dead, fire trucks hosed the blood off the sidewalk.  
 She does not know how she found sleep again after that.  
 Albrecht is a University of Minnesota student living in Dinkytown, a neighborhood heavily populated by Gophers.  
 From 2019 to 2024, the number of gunshot wounds tripled, and aggravated assault cases increased by 41% in the neighborhood, according to the Minnesota Star Tribune . But in the last two years, the number of shots-fired calls in Ward 2, where Dinkytown is located, has decreased by 20% .  
 Ella Albrecht witnessed the aftermath of a shooting that killed one on Halloween night last year. “It’s just sad,” Albrecht said. “It’s sad that a bunch of students our age have to witness that, because we’re so young, we’re still adjusting.” | Photo courtesy of Ella Albrecht. 
 “It’s just sad,” Albrecht said. “It’s sad that a bunch of students our age have to witness that, because we’re so young, we’re still adjusting.” 
 The chief prosecutor of serious crime in Dinkytown is the Hennepin County Attorney, the elected official most responsible for public safety approaches in the county. The prosecutor sets the standards of what is considered murder, who deserves to go to jail for it, for how long and similar critical decisions.  
 Two candidates are in a tight race for that position in the 2026 midterms on Nov. 3. 
 Like most students who live and party in Dinkytown, Albrecht did not know the race existed. She had not heard of Anders Folk or Cedrick Frazier. And she did not plan to vote.  
 Students care, but do not know the solution 
 Only two out of 26 students informally surveyed at the University of Minnesota were aware of the Hennepin County Attorney’s race, but many expressed concern about public safety on and around campus when asked. 
 Folk, the former acting U.S. Attorney for Minnesota, faces off against Frazier, a three-term state representative from New Hope, to replace Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty.  
 Hennepin County Attorney candidate Anders Folk celebrates his door knock launch at his campaign office on Oct. 17, accompanied by Mayor Jacob Frey and Hennepin County Sheriff Dawanna Witt. “This is the largest prosecution office in the state of Minnesota. Maybe we should have an experienced prosecutor run it,” he said. | Photo courtesy of Folk Media. 
 The more moderate Folk, endorsed by Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey, signed the federal indictment charging Derek Chauvin with violating George Floyd’s civil rights in 2020.  
 He is running on his experience as a federal prosecutor and said his number one priority is prosecuting repeat, violent criminals with a focus on balancing consequences and compassion for criminal behavior.  
 Cedrick Frazier, seen as the more progressive choice, earned the endorsement of the Hennepin County Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party. He serves as the vice chair of the state legislature’s Public Safety committee. 
 Frazier checks into the University’s Territorial Hall in a doorknocking campaign to connect with student voters on Oct. 26, 2026. (Image by Maddie Mullikin ) 
 He is running on building positive relationships between the branches of state government, and said his goal is to find solutions to violence outside of the mere prosecution of criminals by focusing on systemic issues that incite crime.  
 The Hennepin County Attorney’s Office both influences and works alongside Hennepin County’s police departments. The University’s is no exception. 
 University of Minnesota Police Department Chief Michael Davis said his department’s policy for crime in Dinkytown is a personal one, focused on building first-name relationships with students as a means to respond to violence more positively. He said that will continue regardless of whether Folk or Frazier is elected.  
 “It’s never really boiled down to who winds up being in that chair,” Davis said. “It’s more about: Are we engaging in the right tactics to dissuade [violence] from happening in the first place?” 
 Although the number of gunshots echoing through the Dinkytown nights has decreased throughout the last two years, the threat of criminal violence remains visceral for college students.  
 Almost a year after a person was fatally shot outside Albrecht’s apartment, her roommate, Emersyn Lokken, was jolted awake at 2 a.m. by gunfire erupting from the same street corner.  
 “That’s where his leg sat and the blood pooled,” Lokken said, pointing from their balcony. “I was freaking out, but I couldn’t stop looking.” 
 A 2:00 a.m. pizza run scares them now.  
 “To this day, when that ice machine goes off, I’m scared,” Lokken said as she gestured to the small gray box across their kitchen. “I do genuinely think I hear guns sometimes. I shouldn’t have that thought. I shouldn’t have the first noise I hear to think that someone’s getting killed.” 
 She also had no idea the Hennepin County Attorney’s race existed. 
 Dan Myers, a political science professor at the University, researches how communication affects voters’ decision-making. He said the nationalization of political media coverage has undermined the importance of local elections, such as the Attorney’s race.  
 “You have to work hard to even be aware these elections exist,” Myers said.  
 Students pessimistic about the impact of their vote 
 University law professor Francis Shen dropped out of the Hennepin County Attorney’s race in April, letting go of a campaign that broadcast public safety policy as his main concern. 
 He recalled a student on his campaign telling him her car had been stolen three times from the campus area – the third found in a ditch, full of bullet holes.  
 Shen said students often do not even call in a stolen car because they feel a police response will not get them any closer to seeing their car again. 
 “What kind of world is that?” he said, “Where someone’s car is getting stolen, and there’s so much lack of faith in the system that we don’t even call it in to someone? … Because if you don’t feel safe, you aren’t safe, no matter what the statistics say.”  
 When it comes to car theft in Ward 2, the last two years have seen a 13% decrease — accompanying the lowering statistics of shots fired in Dinkytown. But students in the neighborhood still live in the fear of crime and bloodshed.  
 “I hear gunshots, and I’m like, ‘Just another night in Dinky!’” Hailey Anchor, a student who has called the area home for three years but is not optimistic about politics providing a solution to the violence, said. 
 Katie Bruss, a health sciences major from Milwaukee, also fears for her safety in Dinkytown, but doubts that voting in the midterms would create change.  
 “I don’t really know what local politics could entirely do about that,” she said. “I feel like it’s more of a systemic issue.” 
 Howard Lavine, a political science professor at the University and polarization expert, said a barrier to young people voting is that they see politics as elitist and out of reach for them.  
 After their chemistry lab, roommates Emersyn Lokken (left) and Ella Albrecht (right) walk through campus to their Dinkytown apartment, where they witnessed the aftermath of two separate shootings. (Image by Jo Larson) 
 “All we think is that we’re young students who aren’t going to be able to have much of a voice because what are we going to do?” Lokken said. “Saying one thing isn’t going to change the world.” 
 The candidates’ response to campus concerns 
 Both candidates said creating a deeper relationship between the attorney’s seat and the University is a big part of their strategy to tackle campus violence. 
 Folk said he would embed prosecutors from his office directly into UMPD to speed up the process of evaluating potential criminal charges. 
 “The best prosecutors move quickly,” Folk said. “This whole idea of justice delayed is justice denied; we don’t want cases to be sitting and hanging out there.” 
 Frazier plans on taking a relationship-focused approach as well. He said he would work closely with campus security, community advocacy groups and student groups to find ways that we can be preventative.  
 “I want to hear directly from students what they like to see that would make them feel safer, or things that we can put in place,” Frazier said. 
 If he took the seat, he said he would install a campus liaison to maintain constant communication  and receive feedback on his policies.  
 When it comes to student outreach, Frazier, who braved the rain to door-knock at freshman dorm Territorial Hall one week before Election Day, said, “I’m here now.”  
 “I think it’s important for leaders to get out and talk directly to the people that are going to be impacted by the decisions that they make on a day-to-day basis,” Frazier said. “It’s important for the students to understand what the role of the county attorney is.” 
 Folk agreed. He has door-knocked at apartments in Dinkytown, and his campaign has conducted student outreach by dropping literature off at student housing.  
 “If you want to know your student experience is going to be the best it can be, knowing that you’re protected on campus, this is an election that should matter to you,” Folk said.
